title: How the five markets differ

inOneLine.simple: The same price move can mean very different things in different markets, because what you hold, how you pay, and how much leverage is involved all differ.
inOneLine.balanced: Buying a [[share]] with your own cash is ownership; a forex position at a broker, a [[futures-contract]] or many commodity products are contracts, often with [[leverage]] and [[margin]]. Hours, costs and margin rules depend on the exchange, the broker and the jurisdiction.

explain.simple: When you buy an ordinary share with your own money, you own a small part of a company, and the most you can lose is what you paid. Penny stocks are shares too, but often of tiny companies whose shares trade thinly. In forex at a retail broker, and in futures, you usually hold a contract rather than the thing itself, and you put down margin instead of the full value. That changes everything about risk. Commodities such as gold or oil can be traded in several ways, often through futures or broker contracts. Each market also has its own trading hours and its own costs, such as spreads, commissions, overnight charges and the cost of rolling futures.
explain.balanced: Useful questions for any market: What do I actually hold? Who is on the other side? When can I trade, and when are there gaps? What does a trade cost, in money, both ways? Is there leverage, and what happens when margin runs short? What can make the price jump? The answers differ by product as well as by market: a commodity can be reached through a [[futures-contract]], a broker's contract or a fund, each with different rules. Use the market comparison screen as a map, and check the rules of the exact product and broker before practising.

assumptions: Illustrative prices and margins, not any broker's or exchange's terms
Fictional share at 20.00 USD; buy 50 shares with your own cash
EUR/USD at 1.1000, 0.10 lot (10,000 EUR), leverage 1:30, account in USD
Example index future (fictional specs): 10 USD per point, price 4,000.00, initial margin 2,000 USD
In each case price moves 2% against you
steps: Shares: cost = 50 × 20.00 = 1,000 USD. A 2% fall loses 1,000 × 0.02 = 20 USD, which is 2% of the money you put in.
Forex: trade value = 10,000 × 1.1000 = 11,000 USD; margin = 11,000 ÷ 30 = 366.67 USD. A 2% move loses 11,000 × 0.02 = 220 USD, about 60% of the margin.
Future: notional = 4,000 × 10 = 40,000 USD. A 2% move is 80 points, so the loss is 80 × 10 = 800 USD, 40% of the 2,000 USD margin.
Same 2% move, three very different results. The difference comes from what you hold and how much leverage you use, not from the market's name.

assumptions: Illustrative holding costs, not any broker's terms
Forex: hypothetical overnight swap of −0.80 USD per night on 0.10 lot
Shares bought with your own cash; no borrowing
Example commodity future (fictional specs): 100 units; rolled once at a calendar spread of 0.70 USD per unit in contango
steps: Shares: no overnight financing charge, because nothing was borrowed. Trading costs still apply when you buy and sell.
Future: no nightly charge, but the roll buys the later month 0.70 × 100 = 70 USD per contract higher, plus fees on two trades.
Each market has a different cost of time. Ignoring it can turn a small planned edge into a loss.

explainSimpler: Owning a share is like buying a thing outright. Forex and futures are more like a deposit on a big deal. A small move against a big deal can cost a lot.
commonMistake: Comparing markets by price alone, or by what someone online says about them. Compare what you hold, the costs, the leverage and the margin rules for the exact product you would use, at your broker, in your country.

quickCheck.prompt: You buy fictional shares worth 1,000 USD with your own cash, no borrowing. Price falls 5%. What do you lose?

options.explanation: No: that would be a 50% fall.
Right: 1,000 × 0.05 = 50 USD. Without leverage, the loss is the same share of what you paid.

quickCheck.prompt: What is the key difference between buying a share with cash and holding a futures contract?

options.text: Futures always cost less to trade than shares
options.explanation: No: costs depend on the product and the broker. No market is always cheaper.

options.text: You own nothing; it is a contract on margin
options.explanation: Right: you put down margin on a contract, so the loss can exceed what you put down.

options.text: Shares can only rise, while futures can fall
options.explanation: No: share prices can fall too, all the way to zero.

doItNow.instructions: Open the Fundamental Analysis Lab and go to the market comparison screen. Read the rows on ownership vs contract, leverage, margin and typical costs. For each of the five markets, write one sentence on what you would actually hold and one on what could make you lose more than you planned.
